newsitem.title: UK: Med tankers steady to firm, some see rates climbin.
newsitem.headline: Med tankers steady to firm, some see rates climbin.

text.p: Mediterranean dirty tanker rates were steady to firm on Thursday and some brokers said they looked set to climb further, while Middle East very large crude carriers (VLCCs) also remained strong.

One London broker said cross-Med 80,000 tonne (Aframax) rates had edged up to W110 from W105/107.5 on a lack of tonnage in good activity. "I can see rates climbing to W120 by the end of the week if the current activity continues," he added.

But an Italian broker was dubious and said there was little if any impetus to push rates higher. "Aframaxes are just steady and quiet in Genoa and I don't see any reason why they should rise at the moment," he added.

Mideast/east VLCCs remained at their year high of W75 as brokers continued to see a shortage of vessels over the next week or two. There were also a number of ultra-large (ULCC) fixtures, with the 515,000 tonne Kapetan Michalis said done at W62.5 for a Ras Tanura/Red Sea voyage for Vela.
Meanwhile, the market looked forward to the start of lifting of Iraqi crude under the second period of the U.N. oil for food deal.
Traders said they expected the process of contract signings and approvals to take at least 10 days from June 8, the first day of the renewed programme.

"If you consider one week to sign and approve all the contracts and then two or three days to arrange the first ship, we should see the first liftings from both ports (Ceyhan on the Mediterranean and Mina al-Bakr in the Gulf) by June 18-20," said one regular lifter of Iraqi crude.
But another said inevitable delays meant that exports were unlikely to resume until "well into the third decade."

Other sectors were mainly steady, with West Africa/U.S. Gulf VLCCs at about W65 and Suezmaxes (130,000 tonne vessels) at W92.5. Transatlantic VLCCs were also little changed at W60/62.5, while cross-North Sea Aframaxes remained at W90/92.5.
Fuel oil in northern Europe firmed to W250 from W235 for 25,000 tonne stems, while in the Med they were little changed at W195.

In the Caribbean, 70,000 tonne crude cargoes edged down to W200 from W205. Current rates are down from the April average of almost W220, but well above the 1996 average of W148, figures on Rigos Chartering Inc's Internet site show.
